item.title: Any road is better with good company
item.description:
Lord Captains!
If you enjoy travelling with a group of characters whose stories develop alongside your own, you might like Shadow of the Road - to be released on 12 November 2026.

The Koronus Expanse is upheld by the Imperium's vast and often incomprehensible machinery, whereas Shadow of the Road's Nippon is being transformed by the arrival of foreign technology and the ambitions of the East Nippon Company. In both cases, the cast of main characters find themselves moving through a world where the old order is no longer quite as stable as it once was.



Set in a fantastical reimagining of 1868 Japan, Shadow of the Road is a story-driven tactical RPG about a group of travellers crossing the nation of Nippon caught between tradition and rapid change. Along the way, the companions will grow closer, clash with one another, and react to the choices you make - while turn-based battles will put your positioning, abilities, and initiative management to the test.

While Shadow of the Road doesn't offer the same intensity of deep character-building as Rogue Trader, it is quite deliberate: rather than spending your journey calculating the most devastating combination of abilities, the focus is on mastering the combat and experiencing the story. There are options to build your party and experiment with their abilities - but the journey is more important.

As in Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, the party is more than just a collection of combatants. Each of the companions brings their own beliefs, personalities, ambitions, and baggage aboard, creating relationships that may fracture or deepen as the story unfolds. Your choices help shape those connections as they make their way through a country being transformed around them.

Both games also place their characters in worlds where the supernatural can intrude upon everyday life - although the scale is certainly different. In Rogue Trader, the Warp is overwhelmingly terrifying. In Shadow of the Road, yōkai bring a more mysterious and varied supernatural presence to Nippon, ranging from mischievous spirits to entities that are genuinely malicious and dangerous. That, in turn, allows the characters to interact with the supernatural a lot more closely - without being branded heretics!

If you enjoyed Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader for its memorable companions, story choices, and a world where your actions can leave a mark - perhaps it's time to gather another group and see where the road takes you.

The old world is fading, and new companions await you to take on the new road.
https://store.steampowered.com/app/1173980/Shadow_of_the_Road/


Join Shadow of the Road on the following social platforms for news and more!

And other platforms!

📍 X (Twitter)

📍 Instagram

📍 Youtube

item.title: Beyond the Game: How Owlmates Keep Our Worlds Alive
item.description:
Making a game is only part of the story. Ten Owlmates writers tell us how one unexplained detail can turn into 350,000 words — and how a private idea becomes part of a community.

It is past midnight. Lore is feeding the cats. Then, a scene about Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader’s Calligos Winterscale arrives without warning. By 2 a.m., it is 3,000 words long and on its way to a friend. The next morning, the reply arrives: several paragraphs of all-caps screaming.
Is feeding the cats a reliable writing method? Probably not. But this moment tells us something useful: fanfiction does not always wait for an outline, a desk, or a sensible hour.

For this article, we spoke with 10 writers from Owlmates, Owlcat Games’ creator program:

JaalCreative, Lore, WrathofFran, Holy Lustration, The Evil Scribbler, Leonard, Cawyden, Red Stairs, LoveOfOurOwnFate, and Mags.

We asked them about their first fan stories, their writing habits, the scenes that escaped their outlines, and the responses from readers that have stayed with them.
Did we find one correct way to write? Not even close. Some set daily word-count goals; others stop when a story is no longer fun. Some map every beat, while others insist they are improvising even as they plan. What they share is attention: to the line of dialogue that lingers, the consequences a game never shows, or the character who keeps talking after the screen goes dark.

Where Stories Begin

Several of the writers began inventing stories long before they knew fanfiction was even a word. The Evil Scribbler wrote an episode of The X-Files by hand at age 12. Holy Lustration produced what she now calls a “glorious” Star Wars: The Phantom Menace self-insert when she was 11, after years of staging dramatic masterpieces with Beanie Babies, Jurassic Park figures, and Spice Dolls. Mags wrote Pokémon fanfiction in a double-spaced notebook, leaving room for the many edits to come.

For others, Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader marked a return — or a first. WrathofFran had already published original fiction but had never felt compelled to write fanfiction. Then, after finishing Rogue Trader in December 2023, she decided there was not enough of the kind of romantic stories she herself wanted to see in the game. The conclusion was perfectly sensible: “Guess I have to write it myself this time.”

The Evil Scribbler returned to fanfiction after almost 15 years. Leonard shared a Rogue Trader story privately with a friend before finding the courage to publish; Vows Over Amasec, which was also the first fic he ever completed, took exactly a year to write. Cawyden was 45 when she published her first fanfiction, Immortalium, having been driven by a need to explore the spaces around Heinrix’s romance that the game could not contain. Even now, with the book counting over 300,000 words, she is still working on it.

For many, the game itself often provided a starting point for writing. Several writers returned to the “what if” behind a plot development: What was another character thinking? What happened after the scene ended? What consequences arose later? Others found stories in the game’s branching endings, sometimes using concepts from philosophy and religious studies to imagine a third possibility between two opposing ideas.

The gap does not have to be large. Sometimes, it is the size of a pendant. Heinrix’s official artwork shows him bearing the symbol of the Ecclesiarchy, but the game never explains this. Was it a mistake, a sign of his faith, a psy-focus, or a remnant from his past? For Cawyden, that single unanswered detail gave rise to a whole history. Meanwhile, another story began with a damaged walkway and a huge ice crystal in the Pillars of Viridice — first, the suggestion of an accident, and then, an entire scene.

But not every starting point comes from something the game leaves unexplained. JaalCreative, who has hyperphantasia — an unusually vivid visual imagination — can find the beginning of a narrative in just a few bars of music or a 30-second TikTok sound. Yet even these sudden sparks are often rooted in personal experience, turning a fleeting impression into something a story can grow from.

There Is No One Way to Write

Once the idea arrives, what happens next? This is where agreement ends.

Lore calls the process “organized chaos.” First, ideas become excited conversations with friends and then a mind map filled with dialogue, images, and thematic fragments. Sometimes, a rough “zero draft” comes next. When writing outside the apartment, Lore usually has a chai latte; at home, colored lights around the desk change to match the scene.

Red Stairs takes a more internal approach, rehearsing a scene in their head until it feels ready for the page, then zoning out and letting the words flow. “I basically hallucinate the plot,” they say.

Holy Lustration sets a word-count goal and a regular time, often aiming for 500 words while sitting on the patio trying not to be distracted by visiting wildlife. LoveOfOurOwnFate writes at night, fueled by tea and one song played on repeat, with a deliberately modest target of 100 words a day. Leonard also uses a daily target, but the real planning happens in a large document full of speech-to-text notes and questions: Why would the characters do this? Does it fit their motivation? Is it physically possible in this universe?

WrathofFran can write on a crowded train, between meetings, or after a workout. A chapter usually passes through three or four drafts before reaching a beta reader. Mags describes planning as a flashlight pointed into a dark room: the next part is visible in detail, the ending can be seen in the distance, and the space between them comes into focus as the writer moves forward. Or, in Mags’ other comparison, it is like Gromit laying track directly in front of the toy train carrying him. Both images are probably more honest than simply saying, “I have a plan.”

Characters, meanwhile, are not always respectful of plans. Some writers know the beginning and ending but leave space in between for the characters to “take the wheel.” Holy Lustration keeps unused ideas at the bottom of the document in case the story finds a use for them later: “We don’t delete things in the House of Holy.”  Not everyone relates to this experience, however. For some, characters have never seized the wheel or dragged a story somewhere unexpected. Apparently, such mystical events are optional, and a story is no less real just because its author remains in charge.

So, the characters may or may not stay under control. The word count, however, is definitely less than cooperative. At Fanfare’s End was supposed to be roughly 4,000 words; it ended up being 41,000. A planned handful of post-game scenes grew into a draft of more than 100,000 words. Much Ado About the Lord Captain was expected to take up 100,000 words or so; more than 350,000 words and 50 chapters later, it is still in progress.

Not every unexpected development can be measured in words. While writing for the Rogue Trader Gift Exchange, WrathofFran discovered that Ulfar wanted to narrate his part in saga style. The result was an unplanned passage in Germanic verse and meter — and, naturally, a beatboxed performance by WrathofFran at the reveal.

Making Room for the Story

Ideas are not usually the problem. The problem is time. Several writers described fitting their fiction around careers, family, responsibilities, and the exhaustion that often remains when a free hour finally appears.

The blank page has other weapons. Red Stairs, who grew up with several languages, sometimes has words collide mid-sentence and ends up chasing English vocabulary “like a mad dog.” A rough draft may come quickly, while descriptions of expressions and surroundings require much slower polishing. Editing poses a different problem: the point when every sentence begins to look like a potential mistake. Then, there are the scenes themselves. Leonard has learned that if a scene feels wrong to write, it can simply happen “off camera,” with the story turning instead to its aftermath. Sometimes, what follows an event reveals more than the event itself.

And when motivation disappears? The advice can be divided into two broad camps: step away, or make the next step very small.

Stepping away can mean going for a walk, changing projects, listening to music, and waiting until writing no longer feels like an obligation. Stopping altogether is also an option. If a hobby is no longer enjoyable or socially meaningful, there is no reason to grind it into the ground.

Taking the second path can be as simple as setting a daily goal of 100 words — small enough to meet even on a bad day, but often just what you need to restart the engine. Some writers switch to a future scene, trusting that even imperfect work will give the editing process at least something to shape. Lore uses rewards, favorite food, and conversations with enthusiastic friends to rekindle focus — an approach developed through learning to work with an ADHD brain rather than against it.

Cawyden has a practical answer to the terror of an empty page: do not begin with the perfect first sentence. Begin with bullet points, a piece of dialogue, or the scene that feels most exciting. A story does not have to be written in the order in which it will eventually be read.

The Reader on the Other Side

There was one thing that became impossible to ignore in the Owlmates’ answers.

Ask them about their proudest achievement, their favorite memory, or what keeps them writing, and sooner or later, they stop talking about stories.

They start talking about people. 

Cawyden still laughs about the reader who left a comment that read, in full: “your fic is a drug and I'm an addict *licks her laptop screen*.” “A bit weird,” she confesses, “but... exciting that someone was so eager to continue reading.”

Not every response is quite so loud. LoveOfOurOwnFate remembers opening an email and realizing that one reader had worked through nearly every story they had published, leaving kudos along the way. “I had a little happy cry, I’ll admit,” they said. Others spoke about readers returning to a favorite story during a difficult period, commenting on every new chapter, or simply saying that they could not wait to continue. What stays with the writers is not praise in the abstract. It is the evidence of there being a real person on the other side.

Sometimes, readers even carry a story beyond the page. Lore knew their original characters had found a place in other people’s imaginations when readers began sending unrelated Tumblr posts and Discord messages simply because they reminded them of those characters. Elsewhere, writers discovered their fics being discussed on Discord, saw readers waiting for update notifications, or heard that a story had changed someone’s view of a character or relationship.

Sometimes, the connection outgrows the story itself. A private message from one of WrathofFran’s readers, prompted by a scene that touched something personal, developed into a friendship. They still talk regularly and now hope to meet in person. Other Owlmates told similar stories: they had expected to write quietly in their own corner and instead found friends from around the world.

The Rogue Trader Gift Exchange turns that connection into an event of its own. JaalCreative and The Evil Scribbler create narratives around NPCs, Rogue Traders, and retinue characters, then watch the community respond in real time. Some of their scripts and character interactions have even been performed by the game’s original voice actors. What usually happens one comment at a time becomes a shared experience unfolding in real time. 

This is why the reader is not merely the final step after you hit the Publish button. They become part of what the story does next. The game gives people a world they love; fanfiction gives them a way to keep playing in it together.

Must Everything Be Serious?

We asked whether fanfiction is a “less serious” form of writing. The Owlmates did what writers do best: they disagreed.

Some answered by taking “serious” very seriously. LoveOfOurOwnFate places fanfiction in a much older tradition: Virgil’s Aeneid, James Joyce’s Ulysses, and the many contradictory versions of Arthurian legend all take existing stories and make something new from them. The term “fanfiction” may be relatively modern; the practice is not.

Others questioned why fanfiction should have to defend itself at all. It is usually created and shared for free, in a culture that assigns a monetary value to almost everything people make. It can be silly, painfully earnest, sweet, strange, explicit, or technically ambitious. Most importantly, it does not have to become a product or prove anything to a market.

Red Stairs sees value in fanfiction being less serious in one particular sense. A sketchbook serves a different purpose from a finished painting. Similarly, fanfiction can be a sandbox where writers experiment with form, narrative devices, and familiar characters without recreating an entire world or answering to a publishing house. Less serious does not have to mean less valuable. Sometimes, it simply means more room to play.

The works themselves make the same case. LoveOfOurOwnFate’s logos_ethos runs two narratives in parallel columns, one written largely in decodable hexadecimal. JaalCreative’s In the Event of Matrimony experiments with form inside an arranged-marriage alternate universe. Fanfiction can offer creative freedom and still be formally ambitious.

Mags offers the shortest answer: “Must everything be serious? Is there no room for enthusiasm and whimsy in your life?”

Fanfiction can demand enormous care without becoming an obligation or a product. Seriousness and play are not opposites.

Press Publish — On Your Own Terms

Should a new writer publish? Before that question comes a more immediate one: How do you make the story exist? The Evil Scribbler’s rule is simple: “You have to make it exist first. Perfecting it comes after that.” Start with the scene you want to write. Set a goal small enough to survive a difficult day. Find people who understand what you are trying to make.

But publishing can carry real risks, and pretending otherwise does not help. Red Stairs warns that fear of criticism is not imaginary: people can be cruel, and automated accounts can leave abusive comments for no clear reason. Writers are allowed to restrict anonymous comments, close messages, ignore unsolicited advice, and protect their peace.

Then, for if and when the time feels right, there is Holy Lustration’s answer:

“Do it. Do it scared. Do it with your teeth gritted. Do it cringe. But just do it. You will find your style and your voice, just like you will find your people.”

No one has to press Publish. But after spending time with these writers, it is difficult to dismiss fanfiction as “less serious” — not because every story is polished or every writer dreams of publishing a novel, but because the same curiosity, dedication, vulnerability, and craft that drive any creative work can be found here too.

These stories began in private — with unanswered questions, improvised plans, and sleepless nights. The friendships, Gift Exchanges, and comments came when the stories were shared. The decision remained each writer’s own: whether and when to press Publish.

“Do it. Do it scared. Do it with your teeth gritted. Do it cringe. But just do it. You will find your style and your voice, just like you will find your people.”

No one has to press Publish. But after spending time with these writers, it is difficult to dismiss fanfiction as “less serious” — not because every story is polished or every writer dreams of publishing a novel, but because the same curiosity, dedication, vulnerability, and craft that drive any creative work can be found here too.

These stories began in private — with unanswered questions, improvised plans, and sleepless nights. The friendships, Gift Exchanges, and comments came when the stories were shared. The decision remained each writer’s own: whether and when to press Publish.

item.title: The Feast of Grimnir returns! Patch 6.12.0 patch notes
item.description:
Heroes!

As promised, the Feast of Grimnir event has returned! From August 25 to September 6, venture forth into Karak Dal once again to slay every troll in sight and make Cousin Okri proud! 

For the duration of the event, select the Weekly Event game mode in the Adventure map to launch the Feast of Grimnir mission! Complete the mission to progress in various repeatable Event Quests found in Okri’s Book and receive shillings and chests!

Make sure to also check Lohner’s Emporium of Wonders for time-limited access to previous event rewards, purchasable for shillings!

Without further ado…

Patch 6.12.0 patch notes
Features & Tweaks

  • Feast of Grimnir

    • Updated the Troll Chief's portrait frame to be more fitting to their chieftain status. Now boss phase information is presented similarly to grudge marks.

    • Troll Chief now uses ‘Lord’ damage reduction instead of ‘Boss’. Max health was lowered to compensate, but should overall be a tougher beastie to bring down.

    • Troll Chief health was increased by aproximately 15% in Cataclysm 3.

Fixes

  • Fixed a crash when firewall software blocks connecting to Twitch servers.

  • Fixed a crash when the Necromancer sacrificed a skeleton that had already died in the host or server.

  • Fixed a bug that allowed Necromancer to sacrifice the same skeleton multiple times with enough latency.

  • Fixed several unlocalized strings in the equipment customization view.

  • Fixed a crash that only happened on Mondays when closing the Weekly expedition view while it is refreshing. No, really.

  • Fixed a crash when interacting with a Keep painting around the time there is a seasonal keep change.

  • More fixes on the Skittergate invincibility.

  • Fixed a crash when receiving a reward from the backend while running an older game version.

  • Fixed a bug where runed illusions for Kerillian’s Longbow had lower glow intensity than intended.

item.title: Special Live Event: Shambling Horrors Live Now!
item.description:
Whatever Admonition's been up to seems to be infecting the population. Horde sightings are on the rise, with some districts entirely lost to the shambling horrors. This isn't a case of a single hab-block falling. This is something much darker and could be the herald of worse to come...

The streets are choked with hordes of infected enemies! To make progress in the event, complete missions with the Endless Hordes modifier.

The event is LIVE NOW until September 2! The rewards will be Ordo dockets, Plasteel and Diamantine. Those who complete the last tier of the event will receive a cosmetic insignia.
